comments.author: @notnotandrew
comments.text: To be clear, encrypting model weights with a secret key such that they can only be decoded on-GPU doesn’t kill open source all by itself. It only prevents proprietary models’ weights from leaking and being usable. Open-weight, unencrypted models would not be directly affected - unless e.g. NVidia decides that their higher end GPUs will only run encrypted models signed by verified model publishers. Then we would have a problem. Hopefully, either NVidia won’t do this (doubtful, I bet they and OpenAI are joined at the hip) or some open-source-friendly competitor would spring up (AMD master race?).

I actually don't think compute power will become the limiter to AI.
When we get AI that's intelligent enough, why increase intelligence further?
After its become powerful enough, it needs to become more efficient.
That means it needs to consume much less electricity, it needs to have very high accuracy to avoid adjusting the prompt. It needs to be so efficient that you can run an AI locally on your watch.

Atm, we are able to run it locally on good computers.
So there's a big leap.

So if we achieve a hyper efficient AI that's self sustaining (new species?), the geopolitical point of conflict, namely chip manufacturing and the business/governmental point of conflict, namely GPU's and the protection of their training data in closed source will be obsoleted.

Closed source is just a perverse incetive for OpenAI to get money.

comments.author: @GarrettGalloway
comments.text:
Let's be real, nobody here could run ChatGPT even if the weights were released. You'd need at least two datacenter class GPUs to run the model even if it were quantized pretty heavily. If you were paging to disk, even on high speed nvme, and running between a 4090 and offloading to CPU...you might get 1 token per hour. That's not usable, practical, or even worth it.

In all reality, this is nothing different than what already exists on your cellphones and in your computers already (TPM, SecureEnclave, Trusted Execution Environment, etc.). People have their arms all up in the air getting wild about stuff they can't do and doesn't impact them anyways. Don't like GPU signing? Disable it...just like you can your TPMs, SEs, TEEs, and other hardware signing and certificate stores.

I expect all of the companies jump on board with this. There are few to none that won't be interested in this at all. This is the one step that would make charging money for LLMs practical. If someone or some company is willing to release a model without any form of tie to a GPU certificate, you can run it regardless of whether you have a gpu with or without this additional hardware. This is just DRM for GPUs. I also expect that the communities that have fun breaking DRM will happily focus on these too.

Do I LIKE it? No. Do I understand it? Yes. Do I think it may be a necessary evil to get companies to continue investing in model training and progress? Unfortunately, also yes.

Imho hardware encryption of a model's weights on specialized hardware should be there by design. "Security by design"! - Very good idea!

comments.author: @RobCoops
comments.text:
From a company and national government perspective these rules make perfect sense. The risks of AI are many and can potentially spell the end of humankind as we know it. So adding protection mechanisms to allow only those the government deems worth to develop it makes sense from that perspective. From a company point of view if you want to win the AI arms race you must keep the secret sauce secret its simpel as that there are no other options to winning this game.

Now there is no reason why an open source group could not build their own AI, which is very costly and time consuming but technically the way to do it is well understood and not overly complicated compared to the other feats achieved by the open source community over the years. There is no reason why if it is all open source these same techniques should be used to protect against the rest of the world seeing everything (that is after all kind of the idea behind open source).
I think the biggest fear from the open source community is the time and cost that it would require to truly build a model like OpenAI's from the ground up. These costs are astronomical and without some way to have these investments pay off for those investing in them not likely to happen any time soon. Which is why many suspect OpenAI and or their competitors will achieve AGI long before any open source initiative can even come close. Couple that with the strong believe that once AGI has been achieved it is game over for all other groups working towards the same goal and the fear in the open source community that these sorts of steps would lock them out of the battle make kind of sense.

Then again when we look at history and we look at the VCR, the car, the bike or electricity or steam engines. We see time and time again that there are multiple people/teams that end up roughly at the same result roughly at the same time and generally it takes a few years or even decades of continuous improvement and strong competition before anyone of the initial designs ends up winning out and by then there are many different organizations that are able to produce this design and build on top of it.
There is no real reason to think that AGI would not follow a similar path...
Lets assume that the rumors are true and OpenAI did birth an AGI, clearly it is not the single sum game that people seem to think since if the rumors are to be believed they did so a few months ago yet no major changes in the balance of power or the global economy have been observed. Even more unlike the predictions they are not exploiting this new supposedly far superior intelligence to gain infinite wealth and fame. To make things more interesting the are going ahead with the single largest IT project in human history building a massive compute capability which is a major investment which if the AGI doom predictions are to be believed would make no sense what so ever if they already have achieved AGI.

My conclusion is that they might very well have something that is close to AGI or even something that would be called AGI by our current idea's of what that would look like. But for what ever reason is is not as capable as they would like it to be, maybe it is just lacking compute power and though it does have all the hallmarks of AGI it is way to slow to be practical. This would make the massive investment in more compute a quite logical step and it would also explain why they are keeping their cards close to their chest when it comes to their achievements. It could even explain the weird period in OpenAI's recent history where the board attempted a coup and the person leading the AI safety and alignment efforts seemingly freaked out and now seems to have disappeared from the public stage.

I am not saying any of this is true but just going by the rumors the behaviors and the future plans it would seem AGI might already be here but it is not (yet) the fastest thinker out there and will need an amount of computational power that will make the current super computers look like children's toys before it might just be able to become useful. My guess for an AGI that is as scary as the preachers of doom believe it will be is at least another 5 to 10 years just to build out the compute needed to power the darn thing. At which point the cost will be so high that it will still take a few decades more before it will become cost effective enough to make a serious dent in the world economy.
